title: Ethiopian English University Entrance Practice Test 6 2024
description: Ethiopian English University Entrance Practice Test 6 2024 featuring 100 authentic questions with step-by-step solutions. Designed for Ethiopian national exam mastery.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly compares the two laboratories?
options: Laboratory A is more modern than Laboratory B.
Laboratory A is most modern than Laboratory B.
Laboratory A is the more modernest than Laboratory B.
Laboratory A is as more modern as Laboratory B.
questions.explanation: Two things require the comparative form: more modern than.

questions.questionText: Of the four candidates, Hana is ___ at solving complex problems.
options: more efficient
the most efficient
most efficiently
efficienter
questions.explanation: A group of four requires the superlative: the most efficient.

questions.questionText: The second proposal is ___ practical than the first, although it is considerably more expensive.
options: most
the most
more
as
questions.explanation: Two proposals require the comparative more practical.

questions.questionText: Which sentence uses the positive degree correctly?
options: The second machine is faster.
The second machine is the fastest.
The machine is fast.
The second machine is more fast.
questions.explanation: Fast is the basic, non-comparative positive form.

questions.questionText: The blue route is ___ than the red route, but it takes longer because of traffic.
options: short
shorter
shortest
more shortest
questions.explanation: A comparison between two routes requires shorter than.

questions.questionText: Among the five roads, this is ___ route to the airport.
options: shorter
the shorter
the shortest
most short
questions.explanation: Among five roads, the superlative is required.

questions.questionText: Which form correctly completes the sequence: large → ___ → ___?
options: larger / largest
largeer / largeest
more large / most large
larger / most large
questions.explanation: Adjectives ending in -e take -r and -st.

questions.questionText: Which form correctly completes the sequence: happy → ___ → ___?
options: happyer / happyest
more happy / most happy
happier / happiest
happyer / happiest
questions.explanation: With consonant + y, y changes to i before -er and -est.

questions.questionText: Which form correctly completes the sequence: thin → ___ → ___?
options: thiner / thinest
thinner / thinnest
more thin / most thin
thinier / thiniest
questions.explanation: The final consonant is doubled in the one-syllable CVC pattern.

questions.questionText: Which sentence is correctly formed?
options: This road is fastter than that one.
This road is more faster than that one.
This road is faster than that one.
This road is fastest than that one.
questions.explanation: Fast forms its comparative by adding -er without doubling the final consonant.

questions.questionText: The new building is ___ than the old one.
options: more comfortable
comfortabler
most comfortable
the comfortable
questions.explanation: Comfortable is a longer adjective and normally uses more.

questions.questionText: Of all the available computers, this model is ___.
options: more expensive
the most expensive
most expensiver
the expensivest
questions.explanation: A group requires the superlative most expensive.

questions.questionText: Which sentence avoids a double comparison?
options: The revised method is more better.
The revised method is most better.
The revised method is better.
The revised method is more best.
questions.explanation: Better is already a comparative form.

questions.questionText: Which sentence is grammatically correct?
options: This is the most fastest vehicle.
This is the fastest vehicle.
This is the more fastest vehicle.
This is the most faster vehicle.
questions.explanation: Fastest already expresses the superlative, so another comparison marker is unnecessary.

questions.questionText: Which form is correct for the adjective careful?
options: carefuler / carefulest
more careful / most careful
more carefuler / most carefulest
carefuller / carefullest
questions.explanation: Careful normally uses more and most.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly compares the two narrow roads?
options: Road A is narrower than Road B.
Road A is narrowest than Road B.
Road A is more narrower than Road B.
Road A is most narrow than Road B.
questions.explanation: Narrow can take -er, giving narrower for two things.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses the irregular form of good?
options: This solution is gooder than that one.
This solution is better than that one.
This solution is more better than that one.
This solution is best than that one.
questions.explanation: The comparative of good is better.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses the superlative of bad?
options: It was the baddest result.
It was the most bad result.
It was the worst result.
It was the worse result of all.
questions.explanation: The irregular superlative of bad is worst.

questions.questionText: The second examination was ___ than the first.
options: badder
more bad
worse
worst
questions.explanation: The comparative of bad is worse.

questions.questionText: Of the three routes, the northern route is ___.
options: farther
far
the farthest
more far
questions.explanation: Three routes require the superlative.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly completes the comparison?
options: Today I have less money than yesterday.
Today I have lesser money than yesterday.
Today I have least money than yesterday.
Today I have few money than yesterday.
questions.explanation: Less is the comparative form used with the uncountable noun money.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses the superlative form of little?
options: She has the lesser money.
She has the least money.
She has the littlest money.
She has the most little money.
questions.explanation: The irregular superlative of little is least.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses the comparative of many?
options: She has manyer books than I do.
She has more books than I do.
She has most books than I do.
She has moreer books than I do.
questions.explanation: The comparative of many is more.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses the superlative of much?
options: He spent the muchest money.
He spent the more money.
He spent the most money.
He spent the mostest money.
questions.explanation: The superlative of much is most.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses a comparative with than?
options: The second exercise is difficult than the first.
The second exercise is more difficult than the first.
The second exercise is most difficult than the first.
The second exercise is more difficult as the first.
questions.explanation: A comparative is followed by than.

questions.questionText: Which sentence is the most formal complete comparison?
options: She is taller than me.
She is taller than I am.
She is tallest than I am.
She is as taller as I am.
questions.explanation: Than I am is the formal complete structure.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses a superlative?
options: He is tallest student in the class.
He is a tallest student in the class.
He is the tallest student in the class.
He is the taller student in the class.
questions.explanation: A superlative directly modifying a noun normally takes the.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses a possessive instead of the?
options: She is my best friend.
She is my the best friend.
She is my better friend.
She is best friend of mine.
questions.explanation: A possessive can replace the before a superlative.

questions.questionText: Which sentence expresses equal quality?
options: The two machines are as efficient as each other.
The two machines are more efficient as each other.
The two machines are efficienter than each other.
The two machines are most efficient as each other.
questions.explanation: Equality uses as + adjective + as.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly expresses inequality?
options: The red car is not as expensive as the blue car.
The red car is not as more expensive as the blue car.
The red car is not more expensive as the blue car.
The red car is not as expensive than the blue car.
questions.explanation: Negative equality uses not as + adjective + as.

questions.questionText: If A is not as fast as B, which statement must be true?
options: is faster than B.
is faster than A.
and B are equally fast.
is not as fast as A.
questions.explanation: Not as fast as means the first item has a lower degree.

questions.questionText: If a book is not as interesting as another book, the second book is ___.
options: less interesting
more interesting
equally interesting
the least interesting
questions.explanation: If the first is not as interesting, the second is more interesting.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly intensifies a comparative?
options: The new system is much more reliable.
The new system is much most reliable.
The new system is more much reliable.
The new system is most more reliable.
questions.explanation: Much can intensify a comparative.

questions.questionText: Which sentence uses far correctly?
options: The new method is far more efficient.
The new method is far most efficient.
The new method is more far efficient.
The new method is far efficienter.
questions.explanation: Far can strongly modify a comparative.

questions.questionText: Which sentence expresses a small difference correctly?
options: The second option is slightly cheaper.
The second option is slightly cheapest.
The second option is more slightly cheap.
The second option is slightly most cheap.
questions.explanation: Slightly can modify a comparative to show a small difference.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses even with a comparative?
options: The situation became even worse.
The situation became even worst.
The situation became worse evenest.
The situation became even more worse.
questions.explanation: Even can intensify a comparative; worse is already comparative.

questions.questionText: Which sentence shows a continuing change?
options: The weather is becoming cold and cold.
The weather is becoming colder and colder.
The weather is becoming more colder and colder.
The weather is becoming coldest and coldest.
questions.explanation: Short adjectives use comparative + and + comparative.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly expresses a continuing change with a long adjective?
options: The technology is becoming advanced and advanced.
The technology is becoming more and more advanced.
The technology is becoming more advanced and most advanced.
The technology is becoming advanceder and advanceder.
questions.explanation: Long adjectives use more and more + adjective.

questions.questionText: Choose the correct linked-comparison structure.
options: The more you study, the more you learn.
More you study, more you learn.
The most you study, the most you learn.
The more you study, more you learn.
questions.explanation: The structure is the + comparative clause, the + comparative clause.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly completes the relationship: 'The harder you work, ___'?
options: the successful you become
the more successful you become
the most successful you become
more successful you become
questions.explanation: Both clauses require the linked comparative structure.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly completes the relationship: 'The higher we go, ___'?
options: the coldest it gets
the colder it gets
colder it gets
the more coldest it gets
questions.explanation: Higher and colder are both comparative forms in the linked structure.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses a superlative with a defined set?
options: She is the tallest of the three sisters.
She is the tallest in the three sisters.
She is taller of the three sisters.
She is the most tall of three sisters.
questions.explanation: Of is used when selecting a member from a defined set.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses a superlative with a place?
options: This is the best restaurant of the city.
This is the best restaurant in the city.
This is the better restaurant in the city.
This is best restaurant of city.
questions.explanation: In is used with a place or context such as the city.

questions.questionText: Which sentence follows standard school grammar for comparing two alternatives?
options: Which is the biggest, A or B?
Which is bigger, A or B?
Which is most big, A or B?
Which is more biggest, A or B?
questions.explanation: School grammar normally uses the comparative for two things.

questions.questionText: Which sentence follows standard school grammar for three alternatives?
options: Which is bigger of the three?
Which is the biggest of the three?
Which is more bigger of the three?
Which is big of the three?
questions.explanation: Three or more normally require the superlative.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly compares quantities of countable nouns?
options: The second class has less students.
The second class has fewer students.
The second class has lesser students.
The second class has least students than the first.
questions.explanation: Students are countable plural, so fewer is used.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly compares quantities of an uncountable noun?
options: The second tank contains fewer water.
The second tank contains less water.
The second tank contains lesser water.
The second tank contains few water.
questions.explanation: Water is uncountable, so less is used.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses more with an uncountable noun?
options: We need more information before deciding.
We need more informations before deciding.
We need most information before deciding.
We need many information before deciding.
questions.explanation: More can be used with uncountable nouns such as information.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses more with a countable plural noun?
options: She bought more books than I did.
She bought more book than I did.
She bought most books than I did.
She bought more of book than I did.
questions.explanation: More can precede a plural countable noun.

questions.questionText: Which sentence uses most to mean a majority rather than a superlative?
options: She has the most books in the class.
Most students passed the examination.
He bought the most expensive book.
This is the most difficult question.
questions.explanation: Most students means the majority of students.

questions.questionText: Which sentence uses most as the greatest quantity within a group?
options: Most students arrived early.
He has the most books in the class.
Most people enjoy music.
Most children like games.
questions.explanation: The most books means the greatest quantity compared with others.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses as many?
options: I have as many books as my brother.
I have as much books as my brother.
I have as more books as my brother.
I have as most books as my brother.
questions.explanation: Books are plural countable nouns, so use as many.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses as much?
options: She has as many money as her sister.
She has as much money as her sister.
She has as more money as her sister.
She has as most money as her sister.
questions.explanation: Money is uncountable, so use as much.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly compares two amounts?
options: The company has fewer employees but less money.
The company has less employees but fewer money.
The company has fewer employees but fewer money.
The company has less employees but less money.
questions.explanation: Employees are countable; money is uncountable.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses a short adverb in the comparative?
options: She runs more fast than her sister.
She runs faster than her sister.
She runs fastest than her sister.
She runs fastly than her sister.
questions.explanation: Fast forms the comparative adverb faster.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses the comparative of hard as an adverb?
options: He works more hard than his brother.
He works harder than his brother.
He works hardest than his brother.
He works hardlier than his brother.
questions.explanation: Hard forms the comparative harder.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly compares the manner of two actions?
options: She completed the task more carefully than her colleague.
She completed the task carefuler than her colleague.
She completed the task most carefully than her colleague.
She completed the task more careful than her colleague.
questions.explanation: Carefully is a long adverb and uses more carefully.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses the superlative adverb?
options: She works the most efficiently in the team.
She works the efficientest in the team.
She works the more efficiently in the team.
She works most efficient in the team.
questions.explanation: Long adverbs use the most + adverb for the superlative.

questions.questionText: Which sentence contains the correct comparison?
options: He is taller as his brother.
He is taller than his brother.
He is as taller as his brother.
He is more taller than his brother.
questions.explanation: Comparatives are followed by than.

questions.questionText: Which sentence contains the correct equality structure?
options: She is as intelligent than her sister.
She is as more intelligent as her sister.
She is as intelligent as her sister.
She is more intelligent as her sister.
questions.explanation: Equality uses as + adjective + as.

questions.questionText: Which sentence contains a double comparison?
options: The new route is much shorter.
The new route is slightly shorter.
The new route is more easier.
The new route is far better.
questions.explanation: Easier already contains the comparative marker.

questions.questionText: Which sentence contains an incorrect superlative construction?
options: She is the best player on the team.
He is the most intelligent student.
This is the most easiest solution.
That was her greatest achievement.
questions.explanation: Easiest is already superlative; most easiest is a double comparison.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly transforms 'John is taller than Peter'?
options: Peter is shorter than John.
Peter is taller than John.
Peter is as tall as John.
Peter is the tallest than John.
questions.explanation: If John is taller, Peter is shorter.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly transforms 'John is taller than Peter' into a negative equality structure?
options: Peter is not as tall as John.
Peter is not as taller as John.
Peter is not taller as John.
Peter is not the tallest as John.
questions.explanation: The correct transformation is not as tall as.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly transforms 'This book is more expensive than that one'?
options: That book is less expensive than this one.
That book is more expensive than this one.
That book is as expensive than this one.
That book is the least expensive than this one.
questions.explanation: If one book is more expensive, the other is less expensive.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly transforms 'No other student is taller than Hana'?
options: Hana is taller than no student.
Hana is the tallest student.
Hana is taller student.
Hana is more tall than every student.
questions.explanation: No other student taller than Hana means Hana has the highest degree.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses 'one of the'?
options: He is one of the best student in the class.
He is one of the best students in the class.
He is one of the better student in the class.
He is one of best students in the class.
questions.explanation: One of the is followed by a superlative and plural noun.

questions.questionText: Which sentence is grammatically correct?
options: Addis Ababa is one of the largest city in Ethiopia.
Addis Ababa is one of the larger cities in Ethiopia.
Addis Ababa is one of the largest cities in Ethiopia.
Addis Ababa is one of largest cities in Ethiopia.
questions.explanation: The required structure is one of the + superlative + plural noun.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly distinguishes like from as?
options: He runs like his father does.
He works as his father does.
He looks as his father.
He behaves like his father does as a clause marker.
questions.explanation: As can introduce a clause such as 'his father does'.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses like before a noun?
options: She looks like her mother.
She looks as her mother.
She looks like her mother does as a preposition.
She looks as her mother does her.
questions.explanation: Like commonly functions as a preposition before a noun or pronoun.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses as to introduce a comparison clause?
options: He works as his father does.
He works like his father does.
He works as his father.
He works like does his father.
questions.explanation: As can introduce a clause containing a subject and verb.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly expresses a general preference?
options: I prefer tea than coffee.
I prefer tea to coffee.
I prefer tea from coffee.
I prefer tea as coffee.
questions.explanation: The pattern is prefer + noun + to + noun.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly expresses a preference between activities?
options: She prefers walking than driving.
She prefers walk to drive.
She prefers walking to driving.
She prefers to walking than driving.
questions.explanation: The pattern is prefer + V-ing + to + V-ing.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses would rather?
options: I would rather staying home than going out.
I would rather stay home than go out.
I would rather to stay home than to go out.
I would rather stayed home than went out.
questions.explanation: Would rather is followed by the base verb, with than + base verb.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly expresses a preference in a particular situation?
options: I would rather walk than take a taxi.
I would rather walking than taking a taxi.
I would prefer walk than take a taxi.
I would rather to walk than to take a taxi.
questions.explanation: Would rather + V1 + than + V1 is the required pattern.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly distinguishes prefer from would rather?
options: I prefer tea than coffee, but I would rather drink coffee than tea.
I prefer tea to coffee, but I would rather drink coffee than tea.
I prefer drinking tea than coffee, but I would rather drinking coffee.
I prefer tea from coffee, but I would rather to drink coffee.
questions.explanation: Prefer takes to; would rather takes than with base verbs.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses 'more' with both a countable and an uncountable noun?
options: We need more chairs and more water.
We need more chair and more waters.
We need most chairs and most water than before.
We need more chairs and fewer water.
questions.explanation: More can modify both plural countable and uncountable nouns.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly completes the pair? 'There are ___ errors, but there is ___ time available.'
options: less / fewer
fewer / less
fewer / fewer
less / less
questions.explanation: Errors are countable; time is uncountable.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly completes the pair? 'The new system requires ___ money and ___ workers.'
options: fewer / less
less / fewer
less / less
fewer / fewer
questions.explanation: Money is uncountable, while workers are countable.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly completes the comparison? 'This solution is ___ reliable than the previous one.'
options: much more
much most
more much
most more
questions.explanation: Much can intensify the comparative more reliable.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly expresses a weaker comparative?
options: This method is a little more efficient.
This method is a little most efficient.
This method is more a little efficient.
This method is a little efficienter.
questions.explanation: A little can weaken a comparative.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly expresses a stronger comparative?
options: The second test is far more difficult.
The second test is far most difficult.
The second test is more far difficult.
The second test is far difficultest.
questions.explanation: Far strongly modifies a comparative.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly expresses increasing expense?
options: Life is becoming expensiver and expensiver.
Life is becoming more and more expensive.
Life is becoming most and most expensive.
Life is becoming more expensive and most expensive.
questions.explanation: Long adjectives use more and more.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly expresses increasing population?
options: The population is becoming larger and larger.
The population is becoming more larger.
The population is becoming largest and largest.
The population is becoming large and largest.
questions.explanation: Large is a short adjective, so use larger and larger.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly expresses a linked change?
options: The more carefully you plan, the fewer mistakes you make.
More carefully you plan, fewer mistakes you make.
The most carefully you plan, the least mistakes you make.
The more carefully you plan, fewer mistakes you make.
questions.explanation: Both clauses follow the the + comparative structure.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly completes: 'The less time we have, ___'?
options: the more quickly we must work
more quickly we must work
the most quickly we must work
the quicker most we must work
questions.explanation: The linked comparative pattern requires the more quickly.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly completes: 'The more information you collect, ___'?
options: the clearer your conclusion becomes
clearer your conclusion becomes
the clearest your conclusion becomes
the more clear becomes your conclusion
questions.explanation: The second clause needs the comparative clearer.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses 'of' rather than 'in'?
options: She is the strongest of the four athletes.
She is the strongest in the four athletes.
She is stronger of the four athletes.
She is the most strong of the four athletes.
questions.explanation: Of is used for members of a defined set.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses 'in' rather than 'of'?
options: He is the fastest runner of the school.
He is the fastest runner in the school.
He is faster runner in the school.
He is the most fastest runner in the school.
questions.explanation: In is used with an organization or place such as the school.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses a superlative with a period or context?
options: It was the coldest winter of the three years.
It was the coldest winter in the three years.
It was colder winter of the three years.
It was the most coldest winter.
questions.explanation: The notes allow of with a defined group or set.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses the superlative in a school context?
options: Marta is the most careful student in the class.
Marta is most careful student in the class.
Marta is the carefulest student in the class.
Marta is more careful student in the class.
questions.explanation: Careful normally uses most, and the superlative takes the.

questions.questionText: Which sentence contains no comparison error?
options: The new phone is more cheaper than the old one.
The new phone is cheaper than the old one.
The new phone is cheapest than the old one.
The new phone is the cheaper than the old one.
questions.explanation: Cheaper is the correct comparative of cheap.

questions.questionText: Which sentence contains no comparison error?
options: This is the most easiest exercise.
This is the easiest exercise.
This is the easier exercise of all.
This is easiest exercise in the book.
questions.explanation: Easiest is the correct superlative and takes the.

questions.questionText: Which sentence contains no comparison error?
options: He is as taller as his brother.
He is taller as his brother.
He is as tall as his brother.
He is more tall as his brother.
questions.explanation: Equality requires as tall as.

questions.questionText: Which sentence contains no comparison error?
options: There are less students in the morning class.
There are fewer students in the morning class.
There are lesser students in the morning class.
There are least students in the morning class.
questions.explanation: Students are countable plural, so fewer is correct.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses the superlative with a possessive?
options: That was the her greatest achievement.
That was her greatest achievement.
That was her most greatest achievement.
That was her greater achievement of all.
questions.explanation: A possessive can replace the before a superlative.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses the comparative of far?
options: The second village is farther from the city than the first.
The second village is farthest from the city than the first.
The second village is more far from the city than the first.
The second village is farrer from the city than the first.
questions.explanation: Farther is an accepted comparative form of far.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses the superlative of good?
options: This is the better solution of the three.
This is the best solution of the three.
This is the most better solution of the three.
This is the goodest solution of the three.
questions.explanation: Best is the irregular superlative of good.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses the comparative of bad?
options: The second result is worst than the first.
The second result is worse than the first.
The second result is more worse than the first.
The second result is baddest than the first.
questions.explanation: Worse is the comparative of bad.

questions.questionText: Which sentence correctly uses the superlative of little?
options: This group has the least experience.
This group has the lesser experience.
This group has the littlest experience than the others.
This group has the most little experience.
questions.explanation: Least is the irregular superlative of little.
